title: Paint What You See: A Benchmark for Dexterous Visual Tool Use
hook: Ask a multimodal agent to repaint a reference image stroke by stroke and it stalls at roughly half-right — then gets worse the longer it works.
key_points: Names a capability existing agent benchmarks miss: fine-grained, closed-loop visual action where tool parameters come from visual evidence.
EASEL's proxy task is reference-guided reconstruction — the agent incrementally paints a canvas to match a target image.
Also covers semantic tasks: region annotation, handwriting, and path planning.
Across 25 evaluated models, reconstruction similarity bottlenecks at 0.40–0.54 — no model gets close to matching the reference.
Trajectory diagnostics show closed-loop instability: models saturate early or degrade after an early peak.
EASEL-Data, a 440k-sample two-stage curriculum, trains EASEL-9B to a 6.3% relative gain over its base and third place overall.
content_html: Agent benchmarks mostly test discrete choices: click this, navigate there, edit that file. Liu and colleagues argue a whole capability slips through that net — what they call dexterous visual tool use, where a model must infer continuous tool parameters from what it sees, and those parameters directly govern the outcome. Their benchmark, EASEL, makes the setting concrete: give the agent a reference image and a blank canvas, and have it paint its way to a match, stroke by stroke.
extra_html:
What 25 models showed

Reconstruction similarity bottlenecks in the 0.40–0.54 range across every model evaluated — roughly halfway to the reference and no further. More telling than the ceiling is the shape of the attempts: trajectory diagnostics show models saturating early or peaking and then degrading, rather than tightening toward the target. That's a closed-loop control problem, not a perception problem. EASEL's semantic tasks — region annotation, handwriting, path planning — expose similarly sharp boundaries in precision annotation and planning.

Can training fix it?

The authors ship EASEL-Data, a 440k-sample two-stage curriculum for trajectory supervision, and train EASEL-9B on it. It beats its base model by a relative 6.3% and lands third among all models evaluated — a real gain from targeted supervision, and also a measure of how far the frontier still is from the task. Details and per-task breakdowns in the paper.

related.title: An Exam for Active Observers
related.hook: Human vision is a loop — look, form a hypothesis, look again. A new benchmark for that loop leaves frontier MLLMs scoring single digits, while humans average 96%.

related.title: Visual Scaffolds Reveal What VLM Benchmarks Measure
related.hook: Redraw the same spatial puzzle to make its structure legible and accuracy jumps up to 34 points — so was the benchmark ever testing reasoning?

flashcards.prompt: What does the paper mean by "dexterous visual tool use"?
flashcards.back_html: Fine-grained, closed-loop parameterized visual action: the model reads tool parameters off visual evidence, and those parameters directly determine the result.

flashcards.prompt: Why does EASEL use reference-guided painting rather than web or GUI navigation as its proxy task?

choices.text: It tightly couples visual evidence to execution precision, which navigation benchmarks rarely test
Painting is the only visual task where correctness can be scored automatically
GUI benchmarks are already saturated by frontier models

flashcards.explanation_html: Existing benchmarks cover web navigation, GUI operation, and software engineering but rarely target the coupling between what the model sees and how precisely it must act.

flashcards.prompt: What failure pattern did EASEL's trajectory diagnostics reveal?
flashcards.back_html: Closed-loop instability — models typically saturate early in a trajectory, or peak and then degrade instead of steadily converging on the reference.
